name: Imhotep
bio: Chancellor to King Djoser (c. 27th century BCE), traditionally credited as architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, Egypt's earliest monumental stone building. Later Egyptians revered him as a sage and healer, and in time as a god.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Imhotep'

name: Hatshepsut
bio: Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty who first acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, then ruled as king in her own right (c. 1473–1458 BCE). She sent a trading expedition to Punt and built her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hatshepsut'

name: Thutmose III
bio: 18th-Dynasty pharaoh (r. c. 1479–1425 BCE) who ruled alone after Hatshepsut's death. Starting with the capture of Megiddo (c. 1457 BCE), some 17 campaigns recorded in his Karnak annals built Egypt's largest empire in the Levant.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Thutmose III'

name: Homer
bio: Traditional author of the Iliad and the Odyssey (c. 8th century BCE). Whether one poet or many, the epics became the backbone of Greek education and identity.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Homer'; quote: Iliad 1.1, trans. Samuel Butler (1898)
quote: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus.

name: Solon
bio: Athenian lawgiver (c. 630–c. 560 BCE) who cancelled the debts that bound poor Athenians to the land, outlawed enslavement for debt and reformed the constitution, laying groundwork for Athenian democracy.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Solon'; quote: Solon, fragment 18 (West)
quote: I grow old always learning many things.

name: Thales of Miletus
bio: Thinker of Miletus (c. 624–c. 546 BCE), often called the first Greek philosopher, who sought natural rather than mythical explanations of the world. Herodotus says he foretold a solar eclipse, probably that of 585 BCE.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Thales of Miletus'; Herodotus, Histories 1.74; quote: Aristotle, On the Soul 1.5 (411a)
quote: All things are full of gods.

name: Fu Hao
bio: Consort of the Shang king Wu Ding and a military leader (d. c. 1200 BCE). Oracle-bone inscriptions record her leading campaigns and performing rites; her intact tomb at Anyang, excavated in 1976, held nearly 2,000 objects.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fu Hao'

name: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
bio: Teacher from the state of Lu (551–479 BCE) whose ideas on ethics, family and good government, collected by his students in the Analects, shaped Chinese statecraft for two thousand years. He held only minor office in his lifetime.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Confucius'; quote: Analects 15.24, trans. James Legge (1861)
quote: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.

name: Sunzi
bio: Traditional author of The Art of War, the classic Chinese text on strategy, said to have served the king of Wu around 500 BCE. The text probably took its final form later, and his life is known only from later accounts.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sunzi'; quote: The Art of War 1.18, trans. Lionel Giles (1910)
quote: All warfare is based on deception.

name: Zabibe
bio: Queen of the Arabs (Aribi) listed in the annals of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III among rulers who sent him tribute in 738 BCE; one of the earliest Arab rulers known by name. Historians often link her to the Qedarites.
source: Israel Ephʿal, The Ancient Arabs (1982); annals of Tiglath-Pileser III

name: Samsi
bio: Queen of the Arabs (fl. c. 733–716 BCE). Defeated by Tiglath-Pileser III, she fled into the desert, then kept her throne as a tributary under an Assyrian overseer; in 716 BCE she still sent Sargon II gold, aromatics and camels.
source: Israel Ephʿal, The Ancient Arabs (1982); annals of Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II

name: A Bronze Age rock carver
bio: Archetype. Nordic Bronze Age communities (c. 1700–500 BCE), long before the Viking Age, cut thousands of carvings of ships, people and rituals into rock, as at Tanum in Sweden. Their makers' names are lost.
source: UNESCO World Heritage listing, 'Rock Carvings in Tanum'

name: A Bronze Age smith
bio: Archetype. Smiths of the Nordic Bronze Age (c. 1700–500 BCE), long before the Viking Age, cast lurs, shields and the Trundholm sun chariot (c. 1400 BCE) from copper and tin imported over long distances.
source: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Sun Chariot'

name: A deer-stone carver
bio: Archetype. Bronze Age herders on the Mongolian steppe (c. 1200–700 BCE), long before the Mongols, raised carved 'deer stones', often ringed by mounds holding the heads of sacrificed horses.
source: Smithsonian Institution, Deer Stone Project

name: A steppe horse chief
bio: Archetype. By about 1200 BCE herders of the eastern steppe were riding and milking horses, building mobile societies around their herds some two thousand years before the Mongols themselves.
source: Shevan Wilkin et al., 'Dairy pastoralism sustained eastern Eurasian steppe populations for 5,000 years', Nature Ecology & Evolution 4 (2020)

name: Arganthonios
bio: Tartessian king in southern Iberia (6th century BCE), famed for silver wealth. Herodotus says he reigned 80 years, lived to 120, welcomed Greek traders from Phocaea and paid for the wall of their home city.
source: Herodotus, Histories 1.163

name: A Thule umiak captain
bio: Archetype. From about 1000 CE the Thule, ancestors of today's Inuit, spread from Alaska to Greenland in skin boats, hunting whales from large open umiaks.
source: Canadian Museum of History, 'The Thule Culture'

name: A Thule angakkuq
bio: Archetype. An angakkuq was a spiritual healer and guide in Inuit communities, consulted in hard seasons and to keep balance with the animals people depended on.
source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Inuit Religion'

name: Odysseus
bio: Legend. The cunning king of Ithaca whose ten-year voyage home from Troy is told in the Odyssey.
source: Homer, Odyssey

name: Ptahhotep
bio: Vizier to King Djedkare Isesi (5th Dynasty, c. 24th century BCE) to whom the Instruction of Ptahhotep is attributed: advice on modesty, justice and good speech, probably written down centuries later.
source: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 1 (1973); quote: Maxim 1
quote: Good speech is more hidden than greenstone.

name: Ahmose-Nefertari
bio: Queen of Ahmose I (16th century BCE) and the first royal woman known to hold the title God's Wife of Amun, recorded on the Donation Stela at Karnak. After death she and her son Amenhotep I were worshipped as patrons of the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina.
source: Joyce Tyldesley, Chronicle of the Queens of Egypt (2006)

name: Harkhuf
bio: Governor at Elephantine (c. 23rd century BCE) who led four donkey caravans south to the land of Yam. His tomb at Aswan quotes a letter from the boy-king Pepi II, eager to see the dancing dwarf (or pygmy) Harkhuf was bringing home.
source: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 1 (1973)

name: Ramesses II
bio: Pharaoh (r. 1279–1213 BCE) who built Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum and proclaimed victory at Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE), a battle that really ended in stalemate. He later made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, with the Hittites.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ramses II'

name: Sinuhe
bio: Legend. Hero of the Story of Sinuhe (c. 1900 BCE), an official who flees Egypt when Amenemhat I dies, prospers as a chief among the peoples of the Levant, and comes home in old age to be buried as an Egyptian.
source: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 1 (1973), 'The Story of Sinuhe'

name: Nectanebo I (Nakhtnebef)
bio: Founder of Egypt's 30th Dynasty (r. 380–362 BCE). In 373 BCE he turned back a Persian army and its Greek mercenaries in the Delta as the Nile flood rose, then built temples from Philae to the Delta.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nectanebo I'

name: Arsinoe II
bio: Ptolemaic queen (c. 316–270 BCE) of Macedonian Greek descent who married her full brother Ptolemy II; the pair were worshipped as the Sibling Gods. After her death she had her own cult in Egypt's temples, and towns around the Mediterranean bore her name.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arsinoe II'

name: Manetho
bio: Egyptian priest of Sebennytos (fl. 3rd century BCE) who wrote the Aegyptiaca, a history of Egypt in Greek for the Ptolemaic court. Historians still use his division of the kings into thirty dynasties.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Manetho'

name: Antony the Great (Antonios)
bio: Coptic Egyptian Christian (c. 251–356) who gave away his land and lived for decades as a hermit in the Eastern Desert. Athanasius's Life of Antony made him the model for Christian monks across the Mediterranean.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint Anthony of Egypt'

name: A Faiyum portrait painter
bio: Archetype. In Roman Egypt (1st–3rd centuries CE) painters made lifelike portraits in hot wax or tempera on wooden panels, bound over the faces of mummies. Hundreds survive, many from the Faiyum; no painter's name is known.
source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Egypt in the Roman Period'

name: Kosmas Indikopleustes (Cosmas)
bio: Greek-speaking merchant, probably of Alexandria (fl. 6th century CE), who traded by the Red Sea to Aksum and perhaps beyond. Later a monk, he wrote the Christian Topography, arguing for a flat world but preserving rare notes on Indian Ocean trade.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cosmas Indicopleustes'

name: Cleopatra VII
bio: Last active Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt (r. 51–30 BCE), of Macedonian Greek descent; Plutarch says she was the first of her line to speak Egyptian. Allied to Caesar and Mark Antony, she died after Actium and Rome annexed Egypt.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cleopatra'

name: Setne Khamwas
bio: Legend. In Demotic tales of the Ptolemaic period, Setne Khamwas, a fictionalised son of Ramesses II, takes the magical Book of Thoth from an ancient tomb and suffers terrible visions until he returns it.
source: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 3 (1980)

name: Miltiades the Younger
bio: Athenian aristocrat (c. 550–489 BCE) who ruled the Thracian Chersonese, then as one of Athens's ten generals is credited with the plan that beat the Persian landing at Marathon in 490 BCE. He died in disgrace after failing at Paros.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Miltiades the Younger'

name: A Pythia of Delphi
bio: Archetype. For about a thousand years a priestess, the Pythia, spoke Apollo's oracles at Delphi. Cities consulted her before founding colonies or going to war; a few are named in sources, most are not.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Delphi'

name: Eupalinos of Megara
bio: Engineer (6th century BCE) who cut a 1,036 m water tunnel through Mount Kastro on Samos for the tyrant Polycrates. Two teams dug from opposite ends and met almost exactly; Herodotus ranked it among the greatest Greek works.
source: Herodotus, Histories 3.60; Hermann J. Kienast, Die Wasserleitung des Eupalinos auf Samos (1995)

name: Kolaios of Samos
bio: Samian sea trader (7th century BCE). Herodotus says a gale drove his Egypt-bound ship west through the Pillars of Heracles to Tartessos in Iberia; he came home with a profit no Greek had matched except Sostratos of Aegina.
source: Herodotus, Histories 4.152

name: Archias of Corinth
bio: Corinthian aristocrat who, Thucydides says, founded Syracuse in Sicily, first driving the Sicels from the site; later chronographers date it to about 733 BCE. Syracuse grew into the greatest Greek city of the West.
source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 6.3

name: Themistocles
bio: Athenian (c. 524–459 BCE) who persuaded Athens to spend silver from Laurion, mined by enslaved workers, on a fleet of triremes, and won at Salamis in 480 BCE. Later ostracized, he ended his life in the Persian king's service.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Themistocles'

name: Pericles
bio: Leading Athenian statesman (c. 495–429 BCE) who built the Parthenon partly with tribute taken from Athens's allies in the Delian League. He led Athens into the Peloponnesian War and died in the plague that struck the city.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pericles'; quote: Thucydides 2.40, trans. Benjamin Jowett (1881)
quote: We are lovers of the beautiful, yet simple in our tastes.

name: Aristotle
bio: Philosopher (384–322 BCE) from Stagira, student of Plato and tutor to the young Alexander. At his Lyceum in Athens he wrote on logic, biology, ethics, politics and poetry, shaping European and Islamic learning.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Aristotle'; quote: Politics 1.2 (1253a)
quote: Man is by nature a political animal.

name: Hypatia
bio: Mathematician, astronomer and philosopher (c. 355–415) who taught in Alexandria and wrote commentaries on Diophantus and Apollonius. Caught in a feud between the city's prefect and its bishop, she was murdered by a Christian mob.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hypatia'

name: Basil of Caesarea (Basil the Great)
bio: Greek bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (c. 330–379) who, after a famine, built the Basileias outside the city: a hospital, poorhouse and hostel for travellers. His monastic rules still guide Orthodox monks.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint Basil the Great'; quote: Homily 6, 'I Will Tear Down My Barns' (see C. Paul Schroeder, trans., On Social Justice, 2009)
quote: The bread you hold back belongs to the hungry.

name: Phidias (Pheidias)
bio: Athenian sculptor (c. 480–430 BCE) who oversaw the Parthenon's sculpture for Pericles and made two colossal gold-and-ivory statues: the Athena Parthenos and the Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Phidias'

name: Pytheas of Massalia
bio: Greek navigator from Massalia (fl. c. 325 BCE) who sailed around Britain and wrote of Thule, six days north, near a congealed sea. He linked the tides to the Moon. His book is lost; later writers quoted and doubted it.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pytheas'

name: Alexander III of Macedon (Alexander the Great)
bio: King of Macedon (356–323 BCE) who conquered the Persian Empire from Egypt to the Indus in eleven years and founded Alexandria. The cost was vast: Thebes was razed, and survivors of Thebes and Tyre were killed or sold into slavery.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alexander the Great'

name: Guan Zhong (Guǎn Zhòng)
bio: Chief minister of the state of Qi (d. 645 BCE) under Duke Huan. Reforms traditionally credited to him, including state control of salt and iron, made Qi the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn period.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guanzi'; quote: Guanzi, ch. 1 'Mumin' (traditionally attributed; compiled later)
quote: When the granaries are full, the people know propriety.

name: A Shang diviner
bio: Archetype. Diviners at the Shang court (c. 1250–1050 BCE) heated ox shoulder blades and turtle shells and read the cracks to ask the ancestors about harvests and war. Their inscribed questions are China's earliest writing.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'oracle bone'

name: Sunshu Ao (Sūnshū Áo)
bio: Chief minister of Chu under King Zhuang (r. 613–591 BCE), traditionally credited with the Quebei reservoir (today's Anfengtang) in Anhui, one of China's earliest large irrigation works. How much of the story is later legend is debated.
source: Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4, part 3 (1971); William G. Crowell, 'Tradition and History: Quebei, Sunshu Ao, and the Persistence of a Narrative', Asia Major (2014)

name: A Spring and Autumn envoy
bio: Archetype. In the Spring and Autumn period (770–481 BCE) envoys travelled between the rival Zhou states to arrange marriages, alliances and sworn covenants. The Zuo zhuan records many of their journeys and speeches.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zuozhuan'

name: Duke of Zhou (Zhōu Gōng Dàn)
bio: Regent for his young nephew King Cheng (11th century BCE), he crushed a revolt by the Shang heirs and his own brothers and built an eastern capital near Luoyang. Confucius revered him as the model minister.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zhougong'

name: Yu the Great (Dà Yǔ)
bio: Legend. Yu, traditional founder of the Xia dynasty, is said to have tamed the great floods by dredging channels to lead the water to the sea, working thirteen years and passing his own door three times without going in.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Da Yu'; Mencius 3A.4

name: Wei Qing (Wèi Qīng)
bio: Han general (d. 106 BCE), born the son of a servant, who led seven campaigns against the Xiongnu for Emperor Wu, including the 119 BCE drive north of the Gobi. The wars cost both sides huge numbers of men and horses.
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, ch. 111

name: Wu Zetian (Wǔ Zétiān)
bio: The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name (r. 690–705). She widened the civil-service examinations and raised officials from outside the old aristocracy, but also ruled through informers and purges.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Wuhou'

name: Zhang Heng (Zhāng Héng)
bio: Han astronomer, mathematician and poet (78–139) who built a water-driven armillary sphere and, in 132, a seismoscope said to show the direction of distant earthquakes.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zhang Heng'

name: Xuanzang (Xuánzàng)
bio: Buddhist monk (602–664) who left China in defiance of a travel ban and walked to India to study at Nalanda. He returned in 645 with hundreds of texts, spent his last years translating them, and wrote a record of the lands he crossed.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Xuanzang'

name: Li Bing (Lǐ Bīng)
bio: Qin governor of Shu (3rd century BCE) who built the Dujiangyan, splitting the Min River with an artificial levee to water the Chengdu plain without a dam. It still irrigates the plain today.
source: UNESCO World Heritage listing, 'Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System'; quote: the six-character Dujiangyan maxim traditionally attributed to Li Bing
quote: Dig the channels deep, keep the weirs low.

name: Zhang Qian (Zhāng Qiān)
bio: Han envoy (d. 113 BCE) sent west in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu. Held by them for about ten years, he reached Central Asia and returned; his reports of Ferghana's horses and Bactria's markets opened the Silk Road.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zhang Qian'

name: Zheng He (Zhèng Hé)
bio: Ming admiral (1371–1433) of Hui Muslim family, captured and castrated as a boy when Ming armies took Yunnan. He led seven treasure fleets (1405–1433) to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, using force at Palembang and Kotte.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng He'

name: Hua Mulan (Huā Mùlán)
bio: Legend. In the Ballad of Mulan (c. 5th–6th century), a daughter takes her aged father's place in the army disguised as a man, serves twelve years, refuses high office and goes home; only then do her comrades learn the truth.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hua Mulan'

name: Gindibuʾ
bio: Arab leader who brought 1,000 camels to the coalition that faced the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in Syria in 853 BCE. The Kurkh Monolith that records it holds the earliest known mention of Arabs.
source: Kurkh Monolith (British Museum); Israel Ephʿal, The Ancient Arabs (1982)

name: A Taymanite scribe
bio: Archetype. In the oasis of Taymāʾ (c. 8th–6th centuries BCE) people carved inscriptions in their own Ancient North Arabian script. The Babylonian king Nabonidus lived there for some ten years (c. 552–543 BCE).
source: M. C. A. Macdonald, 'Ancient North Arabian', in The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Teʾelhunu
bio: Queen of the Arabs (fl. c. 690 BCE) whose Assyrian title, apkallatu, may mark a priestly role. Sennacherib's army defeated her and her ally Hazael, sacked her stronghold Adummatu (Dūmat al-Jandal) and took her and her people's gods to Nineveh.
source: Israel Ephʿal, The Ancient Arabs (1982); Eckart Frahm (ed.), A Companion to Assyria (2017)

name: A Sabaean dam builder
bio: Archetype. From at least the 8th century BCE the Sabaeans of South Arabia built ever larger sluices at Maʾrib to catch seasonal floods. They spoke a South Arabian language, not Arabic, but their incense trade bound them to Arabia's peoples.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Maʾrib'

name: A Qedarite caravaneer
bio: Archetype. By the 8th century BCE camel caravans let Arabian peoples such as the Qedarites carry incense and spices across the desert to Gaza and Damascus. Assyrian kings demanded camels and incense from them as tribute.
source: Israel Ephʿal, The Ancient Arabs (1982)

name: Karibʾil Watar
bio: Ruler (mukarrib) of Saba in South Arabia (early 7th century BCE). His inscription at Ṣirwāḥ boasts of wars that united the region, including the ruin of Awsan with thousands killed and taken. Sabaeans were South Arabians, not then called Arabs.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sabaʾ'; Ṣirwāḥ inscription (RES 3945)

name: The Queen of Sheba (Bilqīs)
bio: Legend. A queen of Saba who brings gold and spices and hard questions to King Solomon in the Hebrew Bible. The Quran tells of her too; Arab tradition names her Bilqīs, and Ethiopia's Kebra Nagast calls her Makeda.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Queen of Sheba'

name: Khālid ibn al-Walīd
bio: Commander of the early caliphate (d. 642) who campaigned in Iraq in 633, then crossed the Syrian desert to join the conquest of Syria. Sources credit him with field command at the Yarmuk (636), which broke Byzantine power in Syria at great cost in lives.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Khālid ibn al-Walīd'

name: Hārūn al-Rashīd
bio: Fifth Abbasid caliph (r. 786–809), whose Baghdad court became a byword for wealth and for patronage of poets and scholars; he exchanged embassies with Charlemagne. In 803 he abruptly destroyed his powerful Barmakid ministers.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hārūn al-Rashīd'

name: Abū Yūsuf al-Kindī
bio: Called 'the philosopher of the Arabs' (c. 800–870), from the tribe of Kinda, he worked in Abbasid Baghdad, oversaw translations of Greek philosophy, and wrote on mathematics, optics, music and the breaking of ciphers.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'al-Kindi'
quote: We ought not to be ashamed of appreciating the truth and of acquiring it wherever it comes from.

name: Ibn Khaldūn
bio: Historian (1332–1406) born in Tunis to an Arab family from al-Andalus. His Muqaddimah explains the rise and fall of states through ʿaṣabiyya, group solidarity. In 1401 he met Timur outside besieged Damascus.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibn Khaldūn'; quote: The Muqaddimah, ch. 2, trans. Franz Rosenthal (1958)
quote: The vanquished always want to imitate the victor.

name: Rābiʿa al-ʿAdawiyya
bio: Sufi mystic of Basra (d. 801) who, later tradition says, was sold into slavery as a girl and freed for her piety. She taught that God should be loved for Himself alone, not from fear of hell or hope of paradise.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah'
quote: If I worship You for fear of Hell, burn me in Hell.

name: Fāṭima al-Fihriyya (Fatima al-Fihri)
bio: Woman from Kairouan who, later chronicles say, used her inheritance to found the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in 859. It grew into a great centre of learning, often called the oldest university still operating.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Al-Qarawiyyīn'

name: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa
bio: Amazigh-Moroccan traveller and judge from Tangier (1304–1368/69) who wrote in Arabic of nearly thirty years on the road, from Mali and East Africa to India and China. His Riḥla is a key source on the 14th-century Islamic world.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibn Baṭṭūṭah'

name: Aḥmad ibn Faḍlān
bio: Secretary, of uncertain origin, to a caliphal embassy from Baghdad to the Volga Bulghars (921–922), who wrote in Arabic of the journey. He describes the Rus' traders he met on the Volga, including a ship burial, a rare eyewitness view of Scandinavians abroad.
source: Ibn Fadlan and the Land of Darkness, trans. Paul Lunde and Caroline Stone (2012); quote: trans. James E. Montgomery, 'Ibn Faḍlān and the Rūsiyyah', Journal of Arabic and Islamic Studies 3 (2000)
quote: I have never seen more perfect physiques than theirs; they are like palm trees.

name: Zenobia (al-Zabbāʾ)
bio: Queen of Palmyra (r. 267–272) of mixed Aramaean and Arab heritage, remembered in Arab tradition as al-Zabbāʾ. Ruling for her young son, she seized Egypt and much of Rome's East. Aurelian besieged Palmyra; she was caught in flight.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zenobia'

name: Sinbad the Sailor (Sindibād)
bio: Legend. A Baghdad merchant whose seven voyages in the Thousand and One Nights bring him to a whale taken for an island, the giant roc and a valley of diamonds, echoing real Abbasid trade with India and beyond.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sindbad the Sailor'

name: A Bronze Age war chief
bio: Archetype. Bronze swords, shields and rich barrow graves mark a warrior elite in Nordic Bronze Age Scandinavia (c. 1700–500 BCE). The horned helmets from Veksø, Denmark (c. 900 BCE) were for ceremony, not battle.
source: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Veksø helmets'

name: A Bronze Age amber trader
bio: Archetype. Bronze Age Scandinavia (c. 1700–500 BCE) had no copper or tin of its own. Its chiefs grew rich sending amber from Jutland and the Baltic south along river routes in exchange for bronze from Central Europe and beyond.
source: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Bronze Age'

name: A keeper of the sun's journey
bio: Archetype. Engravings on Nordic Bronze Age razors show the sun drawn across the sky by a horse by day and carried by a ship through the night, a cosmology archaeologists rebuild from images, not words.
source: Flemming Kaul, Ships on Bronzes (1998)

name: A Bronze Age seafarer
bio: Archetype. Rock carvings across Scandinavia show long plank-built boats driven by paddlers, like the later Hjortspring boat (c. 350 BCE). In such craft people moved amber, metal and livestock along the coasts.
source: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Hjortspring boat'

name: Harald Hardrada (Haraldr harðráði)
bio: Norwegian king (c. 1015–1066) who served in the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard, then ruled Norway harshly and warred on Denmark for years. He was killed at Stamford Bridge while invading England in 1066.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Harald III Sigurdsson'

name: Margaret I (Margrete Valdemarsdatter)
bio: Danish-born ruler (1353–1412) who became regent of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and bound them in the Kalmar Union, crowning her grand-nephew Erik at Kalmar in 1397. She kept the real power until her death.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Margaret I'

name: Snorri Sturluson
bio: Icelandic chieftain, lawspeaker and writer (1179–1241) whose Prose Edda preserves much of what we know of Norse myth and whose Heimskringla tells the lives of Norway's kings. Caught up in Norwegian politics, he was killed at Reykholt.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Snorri Sturluson'

name: Birgitta of Sweden (Birgitta Birgersdotter)
bio: Swedish noblewoman and mystic (c. 1303–1373) whose visions, written down as the Revelations, were read across Europe. She founded the Bridgettine order at Vadstena and pressed the popes to return from Avignon to Rome.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint Bridget of Sweden'

name: A Viking Age shipwright
bio: Archetype. Norse shipwrights built clinker hulls of overlapping oak planks, split rather than sawn, over a keel, with a single square sail. Ships found at Oseberg and Gokstad in Norway are among the finest surviving wooden craft.
source: Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo, 'The Viking Ship Museum'

name: Ohthere of Hålogaland (Óttarr)
bio: Norwegian chieftain and trader (fl. c. 890) who told King Alfred of Wessex how he sailed round the North Cape into the White Sea, and of the furs, walrus ivory and tribute he took from the Sámi. The account survives in Old English.
source: Janet Bately and Anton Englert (eds), Ohthere's Voyages (2007); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'English literature: Old English prose'

name: Leif Erikson (Leifr Eiríksson)
bio: Norse Greenlander (c. 970–c. 1020) who, the sagas say, sailed to lands west of Greenland around 1000 and wintered in Vinland. The Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms landings in North America.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Leif Eriksson the Lucky'; UNESCO, 'L'Anse aux Meadows'

name: Ingólfr Arnarson
bio: Norwegian named by the Landnámabók as the first permanent settler of Iceland (c. 874). Tradition says he threw his high-seat pillars overboard and settled where they washed ashore, at Reykjavík. Settlers brought enslaved Irish captives.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ingólfur Arnarson'; Landnámabók

name: Sigurd the Dragon-Slayer (Sigurðr Fáfnisbani)
bio: Legend. Hero of the Icelandic Völsunga saga and the Eddic poems, who kills the dragon Fáfnir, takes its cursed gold and wakes the valkyrie Brynhildr. The gold brings ruin on everyone who holds it.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sigurd'

name: A Thule bowman
bio: Archetype. Thule hunters carried powerful sinew-backed bows, and in Alaska some wore armour of bone or ivory plates. Oral histories recall feuds between groups; an Icelandic annal says 'Skrælings' killed 18 Norse in Greenland in 1379.
source: Robert McGhee, The Last Imaginary Place: A Human History of the Arctic World (2005)

name: An isumataq (camp leader)
bio: Archetype. Inuit camps had no chiefs with power to command. An isumataq, 'one who thinks', usually the eldest man of a kin group, guided camp moves, work and the sharing of food; people followed him only while his judgment proved sound.
source: David Damas, Igluligmiut Kinship and Local Groupings, National Museum of Canada Bulletin 196 (1963)

name: A keeper of sea-ice knowledge
bio: Archetype. Inuit hunters pass down, by word and example, a detailed science of sea ice, snow, winds, currents and stars, with many terms for kinds of ice, letting people travel and hunt safely far from land.
source: Claudio Aporta, 'The Trail as Home: Inuit and Their Pan-Arctic Network of Routes', Human Ecology 37 (2009)

name: A Thule house builder
bio: Archetype. Thule families wintered in sunken houses of stone and turf roofed with whale ribs and jawbones, entered through a low tunnel that trapped the cold. Their ruins still dot Arctic coasts.
source: Canadian Museum of History, 'The Thule Culture'

name: A Thule ivory carver
bio: Archetype. Thule carvers worked walrus ivory, antler and bone into harpoon heads, combs, needle cases and small figures of people and animals, tools and art that travelled with families across the Arctic.
source: Canadian Museum of History, 'The Thule Culture'

name: A Thule dog-sled driver
bio: Archetype. The Thule brought dog traction across the Arctic: teams of dogs hauling sleds with runners of wood, bone or ivory let families move camp, carry meat and reach distant hunting grounds over the sea ice.
source: Canadian Museum of History, 'The Thule Culture'

name: A Thule pathfinder
bio: Archetype. Around 1200–1300 CE Thule people moved from Alaska across Arctic Canada to Greenland within a few generations, one of the fastest migrations known, following bowhead whales and, some archaeologists argue, seeking meteoric iron.
source: Robert McGhee, 'When and why did the Inuit move to the eastern Arctic?', in The Northern World AD 900–1400 (2009)

name: An iglu builder
bio: Archetype. In the central Arctic, Inuit built snow houses from blocks of wind-packed snow cut with bone or ivory knives and laid in a rising spiral into a dome, so a whole winter village could stand on the sea ice.
source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Igloo'

name: Kiviuq
bio: Legend. Kiviuq is the great wanderer of Inuit stories told from Alaska to Greenland: he travels on by qajaq across the sea, outwits giants and spirits, and marries a fox-woman, on a journey that never quite ends.
source: Kira Van Deusen, Kiviuq: An Inuit Hero and His Siberian Cousins (2009)

name: A slab-grave clan leader
bio: Archetype. From about 1100 BCE, people of the Slab Grave culture in eastern Mongolia buried their dead in rectangular stone enclosures, sometimes reusing older deer stones, as their herding way of life spread west.
source: William Honeychurch, Inner Asia and the Spatial Politics of Empire (2015)

name: A steppe horse healer
bio: Archetype. Horse skulls from ritual sites in Mongolia show the earliest known attempts at horse dentistry, c. 1150 BCE. Later herders pulled teeth that got in the way of the bit, helping make riding and mounted warfare possible.
source: William T. T. Taylor et al., 'Origins of equine dentistry', PNAS 115 (2018)

name: A khirigsuur ritual keeper
bio: Archetype. Late Bronze Age herders (c. 1300–700 BCE) built khirigsuurs: stone mounds ringed by fences and by up to hundreds of small mounds, each holding a horse's head and hooves offered at ritual feasts.
source: Smithsonian Institution, Deer Stone Project

name: A steppe rider-scout
bio: Archetype. Horse remains and milk proteins suggest that by about 1200 BCE herders in Mongolia were riding and milking horses, letting families range farther to find fresh pasture and water each season.
source: William T. T. Taylor, 'Horse demography and use in Bronze Age Mongolia', Quaternary International 436 (2017); Shevan Wilkin et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution 4 (2020)

name: Börte Chino and Qoʾai Maral
bio: Legend. The Secret History of the Mongols begins with a blue-grey wolf, Börte Chino, born with his destiny ordained by Heaven, and his mate, the fallow doe Qoʾai Maral, who crossed a great water to the Onon's source by Burkhan Khaldun.
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, §1, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz (2004)

name: Modu Chanyu (Maodun)
bio: Ruler of the Xiongnu (r. 209–174 BCE), a steppe power centred in Mongolia whose language is unknown. He seized power by having his father shot, built the first great steppe empire, and forced tribute from Han China after Baideng (200 BCE).
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, ch. 110; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Xiongnu'; quote: Shiji ch. 110 (地者國之本也)
quote: Land is the foundation of the state. How could I give it away?

name: Sorghaghtani Beki
bio: Kereit princess (c. 1190–1252), a Church of the East Christian, widow of Tolui and mother of Möngke, Kublai, Hülegü and Ariq Böke. She ran her lands in north China by protecting farmers rather than squeezing them and steered her sons to power.
source: Morris Rossabi, 'Khubilai Khan and the Women in His Family' (1979); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kublai Khan'

name: A chronicler of the Secret History
bio: Archetype. The Secret History of the Mongols, the oldest surviving Mongolian literary work, was written by an unknown author at a great assembly in the 13th century; it tells of Chinggis Khan's ancestors, rise and laws.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'The Secret History of the Mongols'

name: A Mongol böö (shaman)
bio: Archetype. Shamans (böö; udgan for women) dealt with Tenggeri, the Eternal Blue Sky, and the spirits of land, water and ancestors. At Chinggis Khan's court the shaman Kököchü grew so powerful that the khan had him killed.
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, §244–246, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz (2004)

name: A Mongol felt maker
bio: Archetype. Families beat and soaked sheep's wool and rolled it, often dragged behind a horse, into the thick felt that covered gers, lined boots and made saddle cloths, the craft that kept a mobile people housed.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Traditional craftsmanship of the Mongol Ger and its associated customs'

name: A yam relay rider
bio: Archetype. Ögedei Khan organised the yam, a chain of relay stations where riders carrying a paiza tablet took fresh horses and food; urgent messages crossed the empire in days. Local households had to supply the horses and food.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mongol empire'

name: Chinggis Khan (Genghis Khan, Temüjin)
bio: Temüjin (c. 1162–1227) united the Mongol tribes as Chinggis Khan in 1206 and gave them laws and a script. His conquests from north China to Khwarazm destroyed cities such as Bukhara, Merv and Nishapur and killed vast numbers of people.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Genghis Khan'

name: Sübeʾetei (Subutai)
bio: Uriankhai general (1175–1248), son of a smith, who led Mongol armies from north China to Hungary and won at the Kalka (1223) and Mohi (1241). The campaigns he planned sacked the cities of Rus' and left much of Hungary depopulated.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Subutai'

name: Jangar
bio: Legend. Hero-khan of Jangar, the Oirat-Kalmyk epic sung by bards called jangarchi, which took shape perhaps in the 15th–17th centuries. He rules Bumba, a deathless land of plenty where people stay twenty-five, and defends it with his warriors.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mongolian literature'; Jangar: The Heroic Epic of the Kalmyk Nomads, trans. Saglar Bougdaeva (2023)

name: A warrior of the stelae
bio: Archetype. In south-western Iberia (c. 1250–750 BCE) carved 'warrior stelae' show a man with shield, spear and sword, sometimes with a chariot or mirror, honouring a local elite whose names were never written down.
source: Richard J. Harrison, Symbols and Warriors: Images of the European Bronze Age (2004)

name: A Tartessian scribe
bio: Archetype. From around the 7th century BCE, people in southern Portugal and Spain carved the south-western (Tartessian) script on funerary stones, among the oldest writing in western Europe. Their language is still poorly understood.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tartessos'

name: A keeper of El Carambolo
bio: Archetype. At El Carambolo near Seville stood a sanctuary (c. 8th–6th century BCE) where local and Phoenician cults met. A hoard of heavy gold jewellery found there in 1958 may have adorned its priests or sacred images.
source: Museo Arqueológico de Sevilla, 'El Tesoro de El Carambolo'

name: A Los Millares wall builder
bio: Archetype. At Los Millares in Almería (c. 3200–2200 BCE) a Copper Age community raised several rings of stone walls with semicircular towers, beside a cemetery of some 80 passage tombs.
source: Junta de Andalucía, 'Conjunto Arqueológico de Los Millares'

name: An Atlantic Bronze Age trader
bio: Archetype. Around 1300–700 BCE seafarers linked Iberia's Atlantic coast with Brittany, Britain and Ireland, trading bronze swords, cauldrons and tin; matching tools and weapons turn up all along the route.
source: Barry Cunliffe, Facing the Ocean: The Atlantic and Its Peoples (2001)

name: Gargoris and Habis
bio: Legend. Justin's epitome of Trogus tells of Gargoris, king of Tartessos, who first gathered honey, and his grandson Habis, cast out as a baby and nursed by a doe, who taught people to plough with oxen and gave them laws.
source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 44.4

name: El Cid (Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar)
bio: Castilian knight (c. 1043–1099) who fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers, including the taifa king of Zaragoza. In 1094 he took Valencia after a siege that starved the city, and ruled it until his death.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'El Cid'

name: María de Molina
bio: Queen of Castile (c. 1265–1321) who, widowed in 1295, held the throne for her young son Ferdinand IV against rival claimants and rebel nobles, then served as regent again for her grandson Alfonso XI.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'María de Molina'

name: Isidore of Seville (Isidorus Hispalensis)
bio: Hispano-Roman bishop of Seville (c. 560–636) under the Visigoths, whose Etymologiae gathered classical knowledge, from grammar to medicine and geography, into twenty books that served Europe as an encyclopedia for centuries.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint Isidore of Sevilla'

name: Ramon Llull
bio: Majorcan philosopher and mystic (c. 1232–1316) who wrote in Catalan, Latin and Arabic and built the Ars, a combinatorial method meant to persuade Muslims and Jews of Christian truths. He urged missionaries to learn Arabic.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ramon Llull'

name: Gaius Julius Lacer
bio: Architect named in an inscription at the Roman bridge of Alcántara over the Tagus (c. 104–106 CE), built for Trajan and paid for by local Lusitanian towns. Its arches span nearly 30 m, and it still carries traffic.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alcántara'

name: Egeria
bio: Pilgrim, probably from Gallaecia in north-west Hispania, who travelled to Egypt, Sinai, Jerusalem and Mesopotamia around 381–384 and described what she saw in letters to women at home, a rare early travel account by a woman.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Peregrinatio Etheriae'

name: Viriathus (Viriato)
bio: Lusitanian shepherd turned war leader (d. 139 BCE) who survived a Roman massacre of his people in 150 BCE and for eight years beat Roman armies with ambushes and feigned retreats. Rome ended the war by bribing his companions to kill him.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Viriathus'

name: Alfonso X of Castile (Alfonso el Sabio)
bio: King of Castile and León (r. 1252–1284) whose court translated Arabic and Hebrew works into Castilian and produced the Alfonsine astronomical tables and the Siete Partidas law code. His costly bid to become emperor fed revolts.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alfonso X'

name: Bernardo del Carpio
bio: Legend. Hero of Castilian ballads and chronicles who, in some versions, defeats the Frankish paladin Roland at Roncesvalles (778), defending León against Charlemagne. Historians find no real Bernardo behind the tale.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bernardo del Carpio'

name: Amenhotep, son of Hapu
bio: Scribe and overseer of works for Amenhotep III (r. c. 1390–1353 BCE) who directed the king's building, including the mortuary temple whose Colossi of Memnon still stand. A statue says he reached 80. In Ptolemaic times he was worshipped as a god of healing.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Amenhotep, son of Hapu'; Theban Mapping Project glossary, 'Amenhetep, son of Hapu'; Digital Karnak, 'Seated Statue of Amenhotep, Son of Hapu'

name: Peseshet
bio: Old Kingdom official (4th or 5th Dynasty, c. 25th century BCE) whose false door in a tomb at Giza calls her 'overseer of female physicians'. That title is nearly all we know: whether she treated patients herself or managed other healers is uncertain.
source: Giza Project, Harvard University, 'Peseshet (in G 8942)'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Female Physicians in Ancient Egypt'

name: Shenoute of Atripe (Shenouda)
bio: Abbot of the White Monastery near Sohag from c. 385 to his death in 465, whose sermons and letters are the largest body of writing by one author in Coptic. He shielded peasants from abusive landlords, but also led monks to wreck a pagan temple and seize a rival's household idols.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shenute'; Stephen Emmel, 'Shenoute of Atripe and the Christian Destruction of Temples in Egypt', in From Temple to Church (2008)

name: Sappho (Psápphō)
bio: Lyric poet of Mytilene on Lesbos (c. 610–c. 570 BCE) who sang of love and longing, often between women, in her own Aeolic dialect. Ancient critics called her the tenth Muse, yet her books were lost: one complete poem and fragments, many from papyrus, survive.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sappho'

name: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (Hēródotos)
bio: Historian from Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BCE), called the father of history. To explain the wars of Greeks and Persians he travelled to Egypt as far as Elephantine, along the northern Black Sea and through Syria, and wrote down what other peoples told him.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Herodotus'

name: Archimedes of Syracuse
bio: Mathematician and engineer of Syracuse (c. 287–212/211 BCE) who measured the circle and the sphere and worked out the laws of the lever and of floating bodies. His cranes and catapults held off a Roman siege for two years; a Roman soldier killed him when the city fell.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Archimedes' and 'Siege of Syracuse'; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14–19

name: Ban Zhao (Bān Zhāo)
bio: Han historian (45–c. 116) who finished the Book of Han begun by her father and brother and taught at the court of Empress Deng. Her Lessons for Women told wives to be humble and obedient and was used for centuries to keep women subordinate, though it urged that girls be taught.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ban Zhao'; Ban Zhao, Lessons for Women, trans. Nancy Lee Swann (1932)

name: Cai Lun (Cài Lún)
bio: Han palace eunuch who in 105 presented the emperor with paper made from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets. Paper existed before him, but his cheap method helped writing spread beyond silk and bamboo. Caught in a court feud, he took his own life in 121.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cai Lun'; Fan Ye, Hou Hanshu, ch. 78

name: Shen Kuo (Shěn Kuò)
bio: Song official and astronomer (1031–1095). Banished after a defeat by the Tangut Xia, he wrote the Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088), with the first known description of the magnetic compass and of movable type, and an explanation of fossils as the remains of ancient life.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shen Kuo' and 'Mengxi bitan'

name: al-Khansāʾ (Tumāḍir bint ʿAmr)
bio: Poet of the Banu Sulaym (d. after 630) whose elegies for her brothers Ṣakhr and Muʿāwiya, both killed in tribal fighting, made her the most celebrated poet of her day. Later critics ranked her the greatest woman poet in Arabic, and her laments shaped the elegy form.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'al-Khansāʾ' and 'Arabic literature: Elegy'

name: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen)
bio: Mathematician and physicist born in Basra (c. 965–c. 1040), of Arab or possibly Persian family, who worked in Cairo. His Book of Optics argued from experiments that we see by light entering the eye, and his demand that claims be tested made him a pioneer of scientific method.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibn al-Haytham'; Jim Al-Khalili, 'In retrospect: Book of Optics', Nature 518 (2015)

name: Zubayda bint Jaʿfar (Zubaidah)
bio: Abbasid princess (d. 831), granddaughter of the caliph al-Manṣūr and wife of Hārūn al-Rashīd, who paid for wells, cisterns and way stations along the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca and for water channels into Mecca. The road is still called Darb Zubayda.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List, 'The Darb Zubaydah' (2022); Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed., 'Zubayda bt. Djaʿfar'

name: Auðr the Deep-Minded (Auðr djúpúðga)
bio: Daughter of a Hebridean chieftain (fl. late 9th century) who, the sagas say, had a ship built in secret after her son was killed in Scotland and led her household to Iceland by way of Orkney and the Faroes. She claimed land at Breiðafjörður and freed some of her slaves.
source: Laxdæla saga, ch. 4–7; Landnámabók (Sturlubók); both written down c. 1250–1280

name: Guðríðr Þorbjarnardóttir (Gudrid)
bio: Icelandic woman (fl. c. 1000) who, the Vinland sagas say, went to Greenland and then to North America with her husband Thorfinn Karlsefni; their son Snorri is the first child of European descent recorded there. Widowed, she later made a pilgrimage to Rome.
source: Saga of the Greenlanders; Saga of Erik the Red; Smithsonian Magazine, 'Did a Viking Woman Named Gudrid Really Travel to North America 1,000 Years Ago?' (2021)

name: Harald Bluetooth (Haraldr blátǫnn)
bio: King of Denmark (d. c. 986) whose great rune stone at Jelling says he 'won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian'. Ring fortresses such as Trelleborg and the 760 m Ravning bridge were built in his reign. His son Sweyn drove him out.
source: National Museum of Denmark, 'Trelleborg's history' and 'The Jelling stones'; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Harald I'

name: Börte
bio: Chief wife (c. 1161–c. 1230) of Temüjin, the future Chinggis Khan. Seized by Merkit raiders soon after their marriage and won back, she bore the four sons who inherited his empire. The Secret History shows her urging Temüjin to part from his rival Jamukha.
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, §§94–118, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz (2004); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Genghis Khan'

name: Khutulun (Qutulun)
bio: Mongol princess (fl. c. 1280–1300), daughter of Kaidu, the khan who fought Kublai for Central Asia. Marco Polo and Rashīd al-Dīn both tell of her: she rode with her father's armies and would marry only a man who beat her at wrestling, winning horses from every suitor who lost.
source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule (1903), on Caidu's daughter 'Aijaruc'; Jack Weatherford, The Secret History of the Mongol Queens (2010)

name: Kublai Khan (Qubilai)
bio: Chinggis Khan's grandson (1215–1294), who founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, built Dadu (Beijing) and ruled all China after a war on the Song that ended in 1279 and ravaged the south. His invasions of Japan, Vietnam and Java failed at a heavy cost in lives.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kublai Khan'; Morris Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times (1988)

name: Urraca of León and Castile
bio: Queen of León and Castile (r. 1109–1126), one of the first women in Europe to rule a kingdom in her own right. She fought her second husband, Alfonso I of Aragon, rebel nobles and her own son's backers to keep her crown; hostile churchmen wrote her history.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Urraca'; Bernard F. Reilly, The Kingdom of León-Castilla under Queen Urraca, 1109–1126 (1982)

name: Seneca the Younger (Lucius Annaeus Seneca)
bio: Stoic philosopher and playwright born in Corduba, Hispania (c. 4 BCE–65 CE), tutor and then chief adviser to Nero. He grew vastly rich; Cassius Dio blames his sudden recall of loans in Britain for Boudica's revolt. Accused of plotting, he was ordered to kill himself.
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lucius Annaeus Seneca'; Tacitus, Annals 15.60–64; Cassius Dio, Roman History 62.2; quote: Moral Letters to Lucilius 7.8, trans. R. M. Gummere (1917)

name: Master Mateo (Mestre Mateo)
bio: Sculptor and master builder who led work on the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, goal of the medieval pilgrim roads, from 1168, when King Ferdinand II of León granted him a pension. An inscription dates his Pórtico da Gloria, crowded with carved figures, to 1188.
source: Catedral de Santiago Foundation, 'The Portico of Glory: Master Mateo's Masterpiece' (Google Arts & Culture)

name: A Thule seamstress
bio: Archetype. Thule women cut and sewed caribou and seal skins with bone needles and sinew thread into layered, close-fitting clothes, with waterproof seams for boots and kayak gear. Without their skill no one could hunt or travel through an Arctic winter.
source: Betty Kobayashi Issenman, Sinews of Survival: The Living Legacy of Inuit Clothing (1997)

name: A whaling captain's wife
bio: Archetype. Among Iñupiat whalers, heirs of the Thule, the umialik's wife was said to draw the whale to her husband's crew by her conduct; she met the landed whale with a drink of fresh water and helped share out the catch. How far back the role goes is unknown.
source: Barbara Bodenhorn, 'I'm Not the Great Hunter, My Wife Is', Études/Inuit/Studies 14 (1990); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'umialik'

name: A watcher of the winter stars
bio: Archetype. Inuit read the stars to keep time and find their way in the long dark. When Aagjuuk (Altair and Tarazed) rose before dawn in December, people knew the sun would soon return. The lore was recorded from Igloolik elders; how old it is, no one knows.
source: John MacDonald, The Arctic Sky: Inuit Astronomy, Star Lore, and Legend (1998)
